title: Leaf Anatomy
summary: A healthy cannabis fan leaf provides the baseline for interpreting plant stress. It identifies leaflets, serrations, veins, midrib, petiole, upper and lower surfaces, stomata, and internal tissues.

title: Photosynthesis
summary: Photosynthesis explains how leaves use light energy, carbon dioxide, and water to produce sugars that support growth. It connects light, CO2, water status, leaf health, and environment.

title: Stomata
summary: Stomata are microscopic pores regulated by guard cells. They connect carbon dioxide entry, water vapor loss, VPD, transpiration, and leaf temperature.

title: Transpiration
summary: Transpiration is water movement through the plant and out of leaves. It links roots, xylem, stomata, humidity, airflow, temperature, and nutrient transport.

title: Chlorosis
summary: Chlorosis means yellowing from reduced chlorophyll. Pattern matters: old or new growth, veins or tissue between veins, margins or full leaf, speed of spread, and root-zone context.

title: Necrosis
summary: Necrosis means dead plant tissue. It may appear as brown spots, burnt tips, dead margins, blotches, or lesions. Dead tissue will not recover, so progression matters.

title: Leaf Curl
summary: Leaf curl describes posture changes including tacoing, canoeing, clawing, drooping, twisting, and cupping. Direction and location narrow possibilities but do not prove cause.

title: Nutrient Symptoms on Leaves
summary: Leaves may show nutrient-related symptoms, but visual symptoms alone cannot confirm deficiency or toxicity. Interpret with pH, EC, feed history, root health, and environment.

title: Pest Damage on Leaves
summary: Pests leave clues such as stippling, webbing, trails, eggs, frass, silvering, chewing, and distorted growth. Identification requires underside and node inspection.

title: Environmental Stress on Leaves
summary: Leaves respond to environmental stress through posture, color, texture, growth rate, and damage location. Many apparent nutrient issues are environmental or root-zone problems first.
